paragraphs.heading: The rule
paragraphs.text: Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity predicts the ground state of an atom or molecule that has one or more open electronic shells, and it rests on observations of atomic spectra. Within a subshell, electrons first go in one per orbital, all with the same spin, and only then start to pair up. Put simply, when several orbitals share the same energy, electrons spread out across them before doubling up. Friedrich Hund found the rule in 1925, and it is an important tool in atomic chemistry, spectroscopy and quantum chemistry.

paragraphs.heading: Counting multiplicity
paragraphs.text: The multiplicity of a state is 2S + 1, where S is the total electronic spin, so high multiplicity means high spin. Each electron has a spin of 1/2, so the total spin equals half the count of unpaired electrons, and the multiplicity is one more than that count. Nitrogen's ground state, for example, has three unpaired electrons with parallel spin, giving a total spin of 3/2 and a multiplicity of 4.

paragraphs.heading: Why it lowers the energy
paragraphs.text: The high-spin arrangement is lower in energy and more stable because its unpaired electrons have parallel spin, and the Pauli exclusion principle forces them into different orbitals. An early explanation said that spreading out kept electrons farther apart and cut their repulsion, but that turned out to be wrong. Accurate quantum-mechanical calculations since the 1970s show the real reason: the electrons screen each other less from the nucleus, so they can get closer to it and feel a stronger attraction.

paragraphs.heading: Filling orbitals
paragraphs.text: Hund's rule puts limits on how orbitals fill in the ground state under the Aufbau principle. Every orbital in a subshell must hold one electron before any orbital takes a second. The electrons in a subshell also line up with parallel spin before opposite-spin electrons start to be added. The result is that filling always gives the largest possible number of unpaired electrons.

paragraphs.heading: Examples in atoms
paragraphs.text: In oxygen, the four electrons of the 2p subshell sit as [↑↓] [↑] [↑], not as [↑↓] [↑] [↓] or [↑↓] [↑↓] [ ]. Manganese, with a 3d⁵ configuration, has five unpaired electrons all with parallel spin, which gives a ⁶S ground state; the 6 is the multiplicity. Chromium is the lightest atom with a ground state that has two partly filled subshells close in energy. Its 3d⁵4s configuration has six unpaired parallel-spin electrons and a ⁷S ground state.

paragraphs.heading: Molecules and exceptions
paragraphs.text: Most stable molecules have closed electron shells, but a few have unpaired electrons, and Hund's rule applies to them. The key example is the oxygen molecule, O₂, which has two antibonding orbitals of equal energy holding just two electrons. Following the rule, its ground state is triplet oxygen, with those two electrons unpaired in separate orbitals. The singlet state, with both in one orbital, is an excited state that is more reactive. In 2004 researchers made 5-dehydro-m-xylylene, the first organic molecule known to break Hund's rule.
